extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded or NIH-applicant biomedical researchers and people interested in NIH funding policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary on preparing NIH grant proposals and on NIH funding mechanisms (R01 modular vs traditional budgeting, Pioneer awards, R37/MERIT, budgeting for inflation, and policy options to change funding distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims: scope and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims should be general enough to require a project (1-2 papers per aim), but specific enough that they are a project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make each aim broad enough to constitute a discrete project (roughly yielding 1–2 papers) while still being specific and concrete so it represents a real, achievable research project. This is presented as a mnemonic for proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular budgeting and cap
rubrics_metrics.description: Modular refers to the specification of the budget for most NIH grant types in units of $25,000 in direct costs. There has been a cap of $250,000 per year in direct costs since 6/1/1999; you can ask for more money per year but then you revert to a line-item type budget (called 'traditional budgeting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer modular budgeting when the project's scope fits within the cap because it simplifies review (keeps reviewers focused on science rather than line-item details). If your true scope requires more than the modular cap, use traditional/line-item budgeting and request the needed funds rather than artificially constraining the aims to fit the modular limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting: account for BRDPI / inflation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Biomedical Research and Development Price Index (BRDPI) or equivalent to understand the decline in purchasing power of NIH grants (example: a $250,000 modular year in 2011 had 69% of the purchasing power of that same award in 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing budgets, adjust for inflation/BRDPI rather than relying on historical nominal caps. Consider that real costs have risen; the author suggests advocating for a higher modular cap (example suggested: $350,000) or switching to traditional budgeting if necessary. Use official BRDPI tables to calculate needed increases to maintain purchasing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pioneer award 'pioneering' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered pioneering, the proposed research must reflect substantially different scientific directions from those already being pursued in the investigator’s research program or elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pioneer-type/person-based awards target investigators proposing transformative, high-impact approaches that are substantially different from existing work. The program supports individual scientists of exceptional creativity whose proposals could produce unusually high impact across broad areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: R37/MERIT: extended support and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The R37/MERIT program awards a highly-meritorious competing award an extended non-competing interval (longer than standard renewal cycles), e.g., converting a five-year award into a ten-year supported interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer funding intervals (MERIT-style) can free investigators to pursue riskier or longer-term work. However, noncompeting reviews still occur and program officers/ICs may cancel MERIT awards midstream for lack of productivity; extended support is contingent on continued satisfactory progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget scope should match actual project needs (do not artificially compress aims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many investigators historically tailored proposals to fit the $250K modular limit; chasing an outdated cap can lead to under-budgeted/under-scoped proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design your aims and scope to reflect the real research required. If true scope exceeds modular cap, use traditional budgeting to request adequate funds. Avoid compressing aims solely to meet an arbitrary historical modular ceiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program design principle: broaden person-based support to reduce grant burden
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed policy approach is to expand person-based, longer-duration support (not just a handful of 'superstars') so more investigators are relieved of constant grant application pressure and can pursue innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a grantsmanship perspective, programs that provide longer, person-centered funding (e.g., expanded MERIT-like awards) are argued to increase creativity and reduce time spent on grant writing. This is presented as a funding-policy desideratum rather than an application-writing rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-out/terminal grants (policy mechanism) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested mechanism to free funds for younger researchers is a 'terminal grant' or phased-retirement grant that pays senior investigators to wind down labs and commit to seeking no further NIH funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If implemented, such grants would have enforceability and design challenges (how to prevent subsequent submissions, how to prevent the senior scientist from remaining on projects as significant investigator, institutional compliance). This is guidance about program design trade-offs rather than direct application-evaluation criteria.
